units.tr: DISSERTATION On the Human Soul and Its Intellective Power,

units.la: THESIS I.
units.tr: THESIS I.

units.la: PLacidè inter nos de summa animæ humanæ consummatione, cujus ignorantia quamvis aliam cognitionem inanem ac supervacaneam reddit, collaturi; priusquam ad ipsam cogitativæ potentiæ contemplationem accedamus, (quo minoricum difficultate intima animæ Rationalis sacra, quantum ejusdem imbecillitas permiserit, penetrare liceat, de animæ humanæ naturâ in communi, prælibare nonnulla constituimus.
units.tr: Since we are to discuss, calmly among ourselves, the highest perfection of the human soul, whose ignorance makes all other knowledge empty and superfluous, we have resolved, before approaching the contemplation of the cogitative power itself, so that we may penetrate with less difficulty, as far as its weakness allows, into the inner nature of the rational soul, to set out a few preliminary points about the nature of the human soul in general.

units.la: II. Anima igitur humana, est substantia incorporea, & spiritalis, humano corpori animando destinata, eique in unam ὑπόστασιν unita, tanquam pars essentialis, ac per illud potentiis suis actiones edens.
units.tr: II. The human soul, then, is an incorporeal and spiritual substance, destined to animate the human body and united with it into one hypostasis [ὑπόστασιν] as its essential part, and through this union producing its actions by means of its powers.

units.la: III. Unde Actus dicitur primus, (quo excluduntur operatio, ἐνέργεια, spiritus, uti Th. Campanella de sensu rerum lib. 2. cap. 4. sentit, & sanguis) intimaque forma perfectionis, denominationis, & operationis intra corpus exserendæ. Intra corpus inquam: nec enim animæ extra formatum suum, quod actu informat, virtute actionem ullam, ut Paracelsus de imaginativa hominis virtute, in occult. Phil. pag.348. & Frag. libr. Phil. de imag. nugatur, emittere, a natura concefsum est.
units.tr: III. Hence it is called the first act (which excludes operation [ἐνέργεια], spirit, and blood, as Th. Campanella holds in de sensu rerum, book 2, chapter 4), and the innermost form of perfection, of denomination, and of operation to be exercised within the body. Within the body, I say: for it has not been granted by nature that the soul, by any power, should emit any action outside the body that it actually informs, as Paracelsus trifles about the imaginative power of man, in Occult Philosophy, p. 348, and in the Fragments of the Philosophy, on imagination.

units.la: I V. Ac in tali quidem actu five forma, (quæ verè & γνῶσις, repudiatà Avenroïs, qui assistentem eam esse perhibet, 3. de anima, comm. 5. & in deftruct. destructionum contra Algazelem subsistens, informat,) Anima vegetativa & sentiens, per omnes actuati partes diffusa est, & cum corporaturæ non expers fit, ad extensionem materiæ extenditur. Scal. exerc. 297. Sect. 1.
units.tr: IV. And in such an act or form (which truly is γνῶσις, rejecting Averroes, who says it is assistant and not subsisting, De anima, book 3, comment 5, and in the Destructio destructionum against Algazel) which informs, the vegetative and sentient soul is diffused through all the parts of the body it actuates, and since it is not without bodily extension, it extends to the extension of matter. Scaliger, Exercitations 297, section 1.

units.la: V. Animæ verò rationali, corpori, mediante spiritu vitali unitæ, tanquam spiritui immateriato, extenfio nequaquam competit: eâ enim datâ, trinâ dimenfione Ratio extemplò onerata terminabitur; Quod fi hoc circumscriptivè in Ubi aut spacio comprehendetur, tumque locationem habebit, five contactum, aut contiguitatem terminorum quantitativorum, quod absonum ; extremitatibus enim corporis, quis unquam spiritum materiâ liberum, inclusum esse dixerit. Quare fi è rei natura loqui velimus, partes ei correspondentes partibus spacii corporei, tropicè saltem affingi poterunt: Tota enim perfectaque est, ubicunque est, & partem extra partem non habet. Porphyr. libr. de occafionib. Unde fruftraneum illud Scholasticorum perplexum fatis Meletema fuerit, Num anima fit in toto corpore, an in singulis partibus tota, & quænam fedesei potiffimum conveniat. Quod fi itaque cum Zabarella, de part. anima. cap. 5. animam extra cor participative esse dicamus, eo sermonis genere non essentiam, sed ἐνέργειας, minùs principes indigitabimus: Si cum eodem cap. 11. expansam, ad extensionem materiæ; operationes ejus per omnes materiæ partes ad habilitatem organi agentem, intelligemus. Quin etiam subtilitatem prorsus inutilem advertemus in illo, quo quæritur: Num ad divisionem Corporis anima quoque dividatur? nec enim hæc ab illo in esse ullo modo dependet, sed de spirituum natura participans, ubi est, totam instar puncti impartibilis esse deprehenditur. Arist. libr. 8. Phys. cap. 10.
units.tr: V. But extension in no way belongs to the rational soul, which is united to the body by means of the vital spirit, since it is a immaterial spirit. For if it were given extension, the rational faculty, burdened at once with three dimensions, would be limited; and if it were comprehended circumscriptively in a where or a space, it would then have a location, or contact, or contiguity of quantitative terminations, which is absurd. For who has ever said that a spirit, free from matter, is enclosed by the extremities of the body? Therefore, if we wish to speak according to the nature of the thing, parts corresponding to the parts of corporeal space can be ascribed to it only figuratively: for it is whole and perfect wherever it is, and it has no part outside part. Porphyry, book on the occasions. Hence that much-tangled question of the Scholastics, whether the soul is in the whole body or wholly in each part, and what seat suits it best, is a futile subject of disputation. But if, with Zabarella, de partibus animae, chapter 5, we say that the soul is outside the heart participatively, by such a manner of speaking we shall indicate its operations, not its essence, and these less principally. If, with the same author, chapter 11, we understand it as expanded to the extension of matter, we shall understand its operations, acting through all parts of the matter, as fitted to the organ. Indeed, we shall also note a subtlety wholly useless in that question which asks whether the soul is also divided when the body is divided; for the soul does not depend on the body in any way for its being, but, sharing in the nature of spirits, wherever it is, it is found to be whole, like an indivisible point. Aristotle, Physics, book 8, chapter 10.

units.la: VI. Ex his colligitur, hominem triplici potentiâ, quæ tanquam accidens ab essentiâ fluat, conspicuum esse, Irrationalibus duabus, unicaque rationis participe, uti jam ante Aristotelem Sallustius Philosophus ex mente Platonicorum præcipueque Procli, cujus discipulus extitit in libr. de diis & mundo docuit. Ita enim ille, cap. 8. ψυχῶν αἱ μὲν εἰσι λογικαὶ καὶ ἀθάνατοι, αἱ ἢ ἄλογοι καὶ θνηταί. Quod si hæ omnes simul sumantur, & ad materiam bene præparatam, nec non ad certum individuum constituendum ultimatam restringantur, Individualem efficiunt formam; quæ Individui principium sola exstit, ac ut illud substantia fit, impertita existentiâ actuali, & singularitate, omninò causatur. Cùm præsertim nec ab efficiente, utpote quæ rei essentiam non ingreditur, Zabarell. l. 1. de propos. necess. cap. 10. nec materiâ, quæ existentiæ largiendæ impotens, numeralem unitatem non efficit. Idem l. de conflit. Indiv. cap. 5. nec tandem, ut Hæcceitatem præteream, specificâ formâ, speciei saltem constitutrice, μᾶλλον καὶ πρώτως ὅσα dependeat. Scal. exerc. 37. Sect. 17.
units.tr: VI. From these points it is gathered that man is conspicuous for a threefold power, which flows from his essence as an accident: two irrational powers and one power that partakes of reason. This was taught even before Aristotle by the philosopher Sallustius, according to the mind of the Platonists, and especially of Proclus, whose disciple he was, in the book On the Gods and the World. For he says thus, in chapter 8: "Of souls, some are rational and immortal, others irrational and mortal." If all these powers are taken together, and are restricted to the well-prepared matter, and to the constitution of a certain individual, they make up the individual form, which alone is the principle of the individual, and which, so that it may be a substance, is wholly caused, bestowed with actual existence and singularity. This is especially so since it depends neither on the efficient cause, as that which does not enter into the essence of the thing, Zabarella, On the Proposition of Necessity, book 1, chapter 10, nor on matter, which, being unable to bestow existence, does not produce numerical unity, the same, On the Constitution of the Individual, chapter 5; nor, finally, to pass over the haecceity, does it depend on the specific form, which at least constitutes the species, more and most primarily (as it were). Scaliger, Exercitations 37, section 17.

units.la: VII. Unde crasse hallucinantur ii, qui individualem animam hominibus denegant, nec omnibus humanæ speciei individuis, unam numero concedunt, afferentes accidentalem tantùm inter personanas differentiam. Audiat Avenroes qui libr 3. de anima comment. 5. unicam numero mentem, unicumque intellectum omnibus hominibus esse, fingit, Scaliger-um Exerc.307. Sect.17. in hunc modum ratiocinantem; Individuum cum sit substantia, necesse est, ut sit hoc, quod est, per id, per quod est. Est autem per animam. Ergo erit individuum per animam. Anima igitur erit principium ejus, quod est: quam nostri Barbari scitissima voce individuationem appellarunt.
units.tr: VII. Hence those are grossly deluded who deny to men an individual soul, and who grant one soul in number to all the individuals of the human species, alleging only an accidental difference between persons. Let Averroes, who in book 3, On the Soul, comment 5, imagines a single mind and a single intellect in number for all men, hear Scaliger, Exercitations 307, section 17, reasoning in this way: "Since the individual is a substance, it must be this which it is, through that by which it is. But it is through the soul. Therefore the individual will be through the soul. The soul, then, will be the principle of that which it is, which our Barbarians have called, with a most apt word, individuation."

units.la: VIII. Nec Platonici, Pythagorei, Esseni, Sadducæi, Bracmani plerique & Cataini, ab errore maximo hoc purgari possunt aut debent, quippe qui verâ ac genuinâ spiritalium cognitione destituti, tot esse animas, quot corpora sunt humana, negarunt: Falsò sibi persuasi de animarum definito numero, à principio universitatis mundanæ, constituto. Ad corporum enim multiplicationem, ipsum quoque principium intellectivum multiplicari, vel è Sacris manifestum est.
units.tr: VIII. Nor can the Platonists, Pythagoreans, Essenes, Sadducees, most of the Brahmans and the Cathayans be purged of this very great error, or ought to be, since, lacking true and genuine knowledge of spiritual things, they have denied that there are as many souls as there are human bodies, falsely persuaded that the number of souls was fixed from the beginning of the world's universe. For that the intellective principle itself is multiplied together with the multiplication of bodies is clear even from the Sacred Writings.

units.la: IX. Sunt autem tergeminæ hæ facultates, partes sive gradus, unius ejusdemque animæ humanæ, non genere aut essentiis, sed actu & objectis indivisibiliter discriminati. Sub mente enim continetur & vegetans & sentiens, non aliter ac in figuris simpliciores & prioritate naturæ præeminentes, ab imperfectis, minusque; simplicibus comprehendi, dato exemplo Trigoni inexistentis Tetragono, & hujus Pentagono, docet Aristot. l. 2. de anima. cap. 3. Hinc illa Zabarellæ opinio, numero eas & essentia, itemque Pererii lib. 6. de rerum princip. & affect. cap. 4. partialiter, cum numero multæ sint, diversificari, eliminanda videtur.
units.tr: IX. These three faculties, however, are parts or degrees of one and the same human soul, distinguished indivisibly not by genus or essence but by act and object. For the vegetative and the sentient are contained under the mind, just as, among figures, the simpler ones, which excel in natural priority, are comprehended by the more imperfect and less simple ones; Aristotle, On the Soul, book 2, chapter 3, teaches this by the example of a triangle existing within a square, and of the square within a pentagon. Hence that opinion of Zabarella, that they are diversified in number and essence, and likewise the opinion of Pereira, On the Principles and Affections of Things, book 6, chapter 4, that they are diversified partially, since they are many in number, seems to be set aside.

units.la: X. Causatur præterea anima ἀλογῳ à corporali agente κατὰ συνωνυμίαν, perfecto, integro, & univoco, quod est generans, & principalis movens totus. Totus in quâ, cùm & de materiâ & de formâ, quæ rationes seminales sunt, aliquid ad generandum exhibere teneatur; è quo virtus activa transit in Instrumentum generationis semen, spumosum ac albidum, vi seminali (quæ Dei ordinatione primâ, in utriusque sexûs, quisenim prohibet specie eadem coalitione, alteratione, & commistione uniri, seminis miscellâ delitescit, exsuscitatur, animam extendit, ac venturæ domicilium parat) infigne, Sociâ existente causa, Calore, cùm Elementari, tùm Æthereo, & Humore. Sicque Formæ illæ binæ, quæ umbra saltem sunt veræ & perfectæ animæ, non de potestate materiæ primùm, sed agentis compositi educuntur, ac per primum sui esse, in instanti producuntur, in materiâ propinquâ, è quâ postmodum emerfio fit. Nec earum ulla actu præexistit, sed à composito, materiæ potentiâ in actum deducuntur.
units.tr: X. Moreover, the soul is caused in the irrational animal by a corporeal agent, by univocal equivocation, perfect, whole, and univocal, which is the generating and principal mover of the whole. Since it is whole, it must supply something for generation both from matter and from form, which are the seminal reasons. From this, the active power passes into the instrument of generation, the seed, frothy and whitish, which, by the seminal power (which, by God's first ordinance, is roused and hidden in the mixture of seed of either sex, for who forbids that the same species be united by coalition, alteration and commixture?), extends the soul and prepares a dwelling for the coming soul, being marked out, with heat, both elemental and ethereal, and moisture, as the cooperating cause. And so those two forms, which are only a shadow of the true and perfect soul, are drawn out not first from the power of matter but from the composite agent, and are produced in an instant by its first act of being, in the nearby matter, from which afterwards an emergence takes place. Neither of them pre-exists actually, but they are brought from potency to act by the composite.

units.la: XI. At Vero Duplicis hujus animæ ejusdemque agendi aptitudinum, virium ac facultatum doctrinam prætermittentes, postquam generalem animæ humanæ contemplationem paucis complexi sumus; eam Facultatem animæ, quæ discretionem nostri ab irrationalibus creaturis efficit, quæ ad Deum proximè nos elevat, mediosque inter æterna ac corruptibilia. Scal. comm. in lib. Hipp. de Infomn. inter genitum & ingenitū, divisibile & indivisibile, æternum ac temporeum, (ipsa mediæ naturæ, quâ commoti Magi Rationem, corruptibili animæ adunitâ, Lunæ cujus pars altera luce mutuatitiâ, fulgida, altera tenebricosa fit; & Prisci nonnulli Protheo assimilarunt. ut refert Steph. Theupolus Acad. Contempl. l. 4. c. 8.) aggressuri; Quid sacris Literis, quídve rationi ipsi convenientissimum videatur: nunquam immemores, sublimitatis, & difficultatis materiæ, nostraeque in iis quæ àmateriâ sequestrata sunt, tenuitatis, de Quiddítate Rationis primò omnium disseramus.
units.tr: XI. But now, having set aside the doctrine of this twofold soul and of its aptitudes, powers and faculties for acting, and having briefly summed up the general contemplation of the human soul, we shall begin to treat of that faculty of the soul which makes our distinction from irrational creatures, which raises us most closely to God, and which stands midway between eternal and corruptible things, Scaliger, commentary on Hippocrates' book On Dreams, between the begotten and the unbegotten, the divisible and the indivisible, the eternal and the temporal. (This is the middle nature by which the Magi were moved, when the rational soul is joined to the corruptible soul, and the Moon, one part of which is bright with borrowed light and the other part dark, and some of the ancients likened it to Proteus, as Stephanus Theupolus reports, Academy of Contemplation, book 4, chapter 8.) Never forgetting the sublimity and difficulty of the subject, and our own slightness in matters separated from matter, let us first of all discuss what seems most fitting to Sacred Letters and to reason itself, concerning the quiddity of Reason.

units.la: XII. Λόγος itaque sive Anima rationalis, Actus est substantialis, spiritualis, homini tanquam pars ejus, essentialiter conjunctus, potentiâ inorganicâ intelligens, ac separabilis.
units.tr: XII. Therefore the reason [λόγος], or the rational soul, is a substantial and spiritual act, joined essentially to the human being as a part of him, understanding by an inorganic power, and separable.

units.la: XIII. Et actus quidem, quotum materiâ, tum ea quæ sunt φύσει composita, sive ea naturæ sint, sive artificis opera, omnesque operationes aliæ, ut Themist. lib. 2. de anima. cap. 4. M. Albertus tract. de anima. 1. cap. 2. &c. docent, excluduntur.
units.tr: XIII. The acts of which the matter is composed, and those which are by nature composite, whether they arise from nature or from the work of an artificer, and all other operations, are excluded, as Themistius, On the Soul, book 2, chapter 4, and M. Albertus, treatise On the Soul, chapter 2, etc. teach.

units.la: XIV. Substantialis præterea, ad removedos actus primos accidentarios, uti sunt Potentiæ, quæ respectu ad suos, unde dimanant actus, obtinere dicūtur. Rari sunt hac ex parte adversarii. Ipse Plato de subsistentiâ rationis ab Aristotele alienus non est. Etsi enim animam intelligentem in Timæo, Phædio, & 10. de Repub. numerum fecerit, etsi circulum & cum Dinarcho, Empedocle, aliisque harmoniam dixerit, non tamen (uti de Aristoxeno, qui reapse animam & sensitivam quidem præcipuè, ex compage viscerum, ac vigore membrorum, sicuti in fidibus ex intentione nervorum effici concordem sonum animadvertimus, existere, delirus senex, referente Lactant. lib. 7. de divin. instit. c. 13. opinatus est,) eam vel quantitatem, vel qualitate esse voluit, sed abstrusioribus his notionibus ad imitationem Pythagoræ ac Philolai, teste Zabarell. de rer. desin. tit. de anima def. divinitatem, perfectionem, multiplicationem operationum, ordinemque, nunquam non decorum ac sibi constantem, indigitare conatus est.
units.tr: XIV. Further, it is substantial, so as to remove the accidental first acts, such as the powers, which are said to belong to the things from which their acts flow. On this point our opponents are few. Plato himself is not foreign to Aristotle's view of the subsistence of reason. For although in the Timaeus, Phaedo, and Republic book 10 he made the understanding soul a number, and although he called it a circle, and with Dinarchus, Empedocles and others a harmony, yet he did not wish it to be a quantity or a quality (unlike Aristoxenus, who, as the mad old man, as Lactantius reports, Divine Institutes book 7, chapter 13, supposed that the soul, especially the sensitive soul, exists, arising from the structure of the viscera and the vigour of the limbs, just as we observe a harmonious sound produced in the strings by the tension of the sinews). Rather, in imitation of Pythagoras and Philolaus, as Zabarella reports, On the Things Sought, title On the Definition of the Soul, he tried by those rather abstruse notions to indicate the divinity, perfection, multiplication of operations, and an order always becoming and consistent with itself.

units.la: Et hanc quidem explicationem & defensionem pii Philosophi etiam contra Aristotelem Commentatores tuentur. D. Thomas in lib. de anima lect. 8. Philoponus in Comment. l. 1. de anima 1. cap. 3. Beffarius l. 2. in Calumn. Plat. Macrob. in Somn. Scip. cap. 15. &c.
units.tr: And the commentators also defend this explanation and defence of the pious philosopher, even against Aristotle: St Thomas, on the book On the Soul, lecture 8; Philoponus, Commentary on On the Soul, book 1, chapter 3; Beffarius, On the Calumnies against Plato, book 2; Macrobius, On the Dream of Scipio, chapter 15, etc.

units.la: XV. Spiritalis est, immaterialis, & incorporeus sua substantia, atque natura actus; etsi conjunctione materialis, eo quod aliquo modo a materia seu corpore, cui unitus est, pendere videatur, dici possit. Quod equidem modus perceptionis abstractorum, & ab omni affectione sequestratorum; nec non volitionis ratio abunde probat:
units.tr: XV. It is spiritual, immaterial and incorporeal in its substance and nature as act; although by its union it may be called material, inasmuch as it seems in some way to depend on the matter or body to which it is joined. Indeed the manner of perceiving abstract things, and things removed from every affection, as well as the nature of volition, sufficiently proves this:

units.la: Anima infit Poeta Stellatus in Libra est individua atq; immaterialis
units.tr: The soul, says the starry poet in Libra, is indivisible and immaterial.

units.la: Et veluti centrum quoddam ad quod plurima tendit Linea; per sensus quia cuncta feruntur ad illam, Ceu fluvii concurrunt undiq; in aquor.—
units.tr: And as a certain centre to which many lines tend, since all things are carried to it through the senses, as rivers run together from every side into the sea.

units.la: Patres e quibus est D. Dionysius 4. cap. de divin. nom. Ambrosius libr. de Noe & Arca, Damascenus 2. Fidei orthod. cap. 12. Augustinus lib. 6. de Trinit. cap. 6. Nazianzenus Apologet. 1. Nyssenus de opificio hominis. cap. 15. passim id testantur. Nec tamen omnino errarunt D. Hieronymus, Athanasius & Basilius, qui materiatum quodammodo corporeumq; vulgari loquendi genere usi, dixerunt; cum non simpliciter, sed comparate tantum in negotio arduo imprimis, quod fuit illis cum famosissimis haereticis, Carpocrate, Cerdone, Priscillianistis, Gnosticis, &c. qui ut refert Irenaeus l. 1. adv. Haeret. c. 24. Theodoretus libr. de divin. decret. Augustin. l. de haeref. c. 70. contenderunt animam nostram intelligentem Dei esse partem, de quo & ex quo emanet: compositione animae nostrae defensuri, loquuti sint. Quod si in se materiata ac corporalis anima nostra cum Cleante, Apollinari Alexandrino, Tertulliano, Stoicis nonnullis ac Sadducæis afferatur, erroneum illud dogma, ac nullo modo tolerandum censebitur.
units.tr: The Fathers, among whom are St Dionysius, chapter 4 of On the Divine Names; Ambrose, book On Noah and the Ark; Damascene, On the Orthodox Faith, book 2, chapter 12; Augustine, On the Trinity, book 6, chapter 6; Gregory Nazianzen, Apologia 1; Gregory of Nyssa, On the Making of Man, chapter 15, bear witness to this everywhere. Nor did St Jerome, Athanasius and Basil altogether err, who, speaking in the common manner, called the soul somewhat material and corporeal; for they spoke not simply but only comparatively, chiefly in the difficult business they had with the notorious heretics Carpocrates, Cerdo, the Priscillianists, the Gnostics, etc., who, as Irenaeus reports, Against Heresies book 1, chapter 24; Theodoret, On the Divine Decrees; Augustine, On Heresies, chapter 70, maintained that our understanding soul is a part of God, from whom and out of whom it emanates. If, however, our soul is taken to be material and corporeal in itself, with Cleanthes, Apollinaris of Alexandria, Tertullian, some Stoics and the Sadducees, that erroneous dogma will be judged to be in no way to be tolerated.

units.la: XVI. Nec corporeorum quidem organorum adjumento intelligit, absoluta fi spectetur, propriaque ejus per essentiam formalis operatio, quæ Intellectionis nomine venit. Quâ enim varia rerum simulacra cognoscit, intelligit, dijudicat: id est, inter agendum ac edendum tales operationes nullo prorsus instrumento egetmateriato: jam tum enim omne usum ac consuetudinem, quæ illi cum sensibus, tum externis, tum internis necessario antea intercedebat, ipso actu terminat. Utpote cum Icones rerum extrinsecus, Phantasiâ, reliquisque sensationibus percerta organa mediantibus, ad fictricem facultatem perlatæ, à mente objectivè tantum adhibeantur, non organicè ceu Medium. Per quod. Intellectus enim operationem suam formalem non communicat cum instrumento corporeo, nec vice-versâ cum mentis actione actio corporalis. Idem disertis verbis exponit Scaliger, exerc. 265. dum ait: Anima non sequitur corpus, ut pessime sentit Galenus, sed ejus substantia, tametsi esse quit sine corpore, tamen dum est in corpore, sine corporeis objectis non potest initiari sacris intellectionis: Ergo ne agere quidem. Movent enim species animam, verùm ratione nondum utentem. Rationes huic stabiliendo recenset Aristoteles, libr. 3. de anima. cap. 4. text. 6. 7. Hinc eam tex. 4. 12. ἀμιγῆ vocat; Immistam, tum ratione objectorum, tum etiam organorum, à quibus omninò absoluta est: cùm munia sua sive Intelligendo, sive Volendo, instrumentis non permista exsequatur.
units.tr: XVI. Nor, if considered in itself, absolutely, and in its own formal operation through its essence, which is called intellection, does it understand with the aid of corporeal organs. For by which it knows, understands and judges the various likenesses of things, that is, in acting and producing such operations, it needs no material instrument at all. For it already terminates, by the act itself, all the use and habit which previously necessarily existed between it and the senses, both external and internal. For the images of things, conveyed from outside through the organs perceived by phantasy and the other sensations to the forming faculty, are used by the mind only objectively, not organically as a medium. Hence the intellect does not share its formal operation with a corporeal instrument, nor conversely does a bodily action share in the action of the mind. Scaliger, Exercise 265, expresses the same in plain words, when he says: The soul does not follow the body, as Galen very badly thinks, but its substance, although it can exist without the body, yet while it is in the body it cannot begin the holy acts of understanding without corporeal objects. Therefore it does not even act. For the species move the soul, but a soul not yet using reason. Aristotle, On the Soul, book 3, chapter 4, texts 6 and 7, recounts the reasons for establishing this. Hence in text 4 and 12 he calls it [ἀμιγῆ], unmixed: unmixed both in respect of its objects and of its organs, from which it is wholly separate, since it performs its functions, whether understanding or willing, without being mixed with instruments.

units.la: XVII. Perspicitur igitur ex hoc, Potentias in anima animâ humanâ duplices esse, quarum altera inorganica sit, altera organica. Hæc operationes suas exercet per instrumenta materiata, ut est videre, sentire, &c. estque in conjuncto, tanquam subjecto inseparabili. Illa longè simplicior est, utpote quæ in ipsa animæ essentiâ, etiam separatâ, velut causâ aut subjecto radicatur, nec à speciebus intelligibilibus jam utens ratio movetur.
units.tr: XVII. From this it is therefore clear that there are two kinds of powers in the human soul: one is inorganic, the other organic. The latter exercises its operations through material instruments, as in seeing, feeling, etc., and it exists in the composite as in an inseparable subject. The former is much simpler, since it is rooted in the very essence of the soul, even when separated, as in a cause or subject; and the reason, which now uses intelligible species, is not moved by them.

units.la: XVIII. Hinc inorganicum illud actionum humanarum principium duplex, à corporibus cœlestibus nihil directè pati dicitur, sed inclinatione saltem aliquâ fertur, astris suâ naturâ, ac per se, in corpora agentibus; quæ ad rationis postmodum officia diversimodè obeunda, non parum faciunt. D. Thom. p. 1. S. T. quæst. 115. artic. 4.
units.tr: XVIII. Hence this twofold inorganic principle of human actions is said not to be directly affected by the heavenly bodies, but at least to be carried by some inclination, the stars acting upon bodies by their own nature and in themselves; and this contributes not a little to the various offices of reason afterwards to be discharged. St Thomas, Summa Theologica, part 1, question 115, article 4.

units.la: XIX. Quoniam verò Entia quævis, Universale illud ante multa, quod est Ens independens, absolutissimum & perfectissimum; participantia, compositionis notâ impurata sunt: In ipso autem Deo αὐτοπροέτω solo, tanquam actu simplicissimo, qui suum esse à nullo acceptum habet, ipsumque singulum omnium rerum perfectiones in se continet, diversum quid ab ipsomet ponere (utpote qui nec prioritatem ullam, nec Accidentia, sustineat aut recipiat) blasphemum est ac impium: Animæ rationali etsi simplex in suo gradu habeatur, omninò absoluta natura, cùm vel ex actu & potentiâ constet, concedi nequaquam poterit. Compositam eam esse, non secùs ac Intelligentias, (à quibus tamen, falsò & inani conatu, reclamante Origene, libr. 1. περὶ ἀρχῶν, specie diversa est) quæ & ipsæ olim mutationi obnoxiæ fuerunt, ac nonnihil materialitatis ac potentialitatis jam nunc obtinent, ratio evincit; S. Literæ stabiliunt.
units.tr: XIX. But since all beings, that universal before many, which is the independent, most absolute and most perfect Being, participating in it, are tainted by the mark of composition; and since to posit in God alone, who is self-existent [αὐτοπροέτω], as most simple act, who has his being from no one, and who contains within himself the perfections of each and every thing, something diverse from himself (since he sustains or receives neither priority nor accidents) is blasphemous and impious, it cannot be granted in any way that the rational soul, though it is held to be simple in its own order, is an absolutely unqualified nature, since it consists of act and potency. That it is composite, no differently from the Intelligences (from which, however, it differs in species, by a false and empty effort, Origen objecting, On First Principles, book 1), which themselves once were subject to change and now possess some materiality and potentiality, reason proves and the Holy Scriptures establish.

units.la: XX. Gaudet immortalitatis nihilominus & independentiæ à corpore, dono, uti verbo suo S. S. Eccles. 12. Sapient. cap. 2. 3. 4. 5. Matth. 22. ita enim explicatur locus iste à D. Chrysostom. homil. 71. &c. Deus expressit.
units.tr: XX. Nevertheless it rejoices in immortality and independence from the body, as a gift, as God has expressed in his own word: Ecclesiastes 12; Wisdom chapters 2, 3, 4, 5; Matthew 22. For thus that passage is explained by St Chrysostom, Homily 71, etc.

units.la: —Hoc principium est fundamentum, salutis Æternam esse animi naturam, & prorisus ab omni Parcarum numero exemtam— ait Paling. in Capric. Nec moramur infantiles illas Epicuri, Democriti, Dicæarchi, Plinii libr. 7. nat. hist. cap. 55. & Machiavellistarum, argutias. Quin potius faniores Philosophos, Ethnicos quamvis, adire ac consulere liceat. Quantâ vi impugnarunt, imo oppugnarunt, Pythagoras, ejusq; Præceptor Phærecydes, Trifmegistus, Zoroaster, Numerius, & in Alcibiade Plato, inhumanam illam dementis annihilatione sententiam? Sallustius libr. de diis & mundo. cap. 20. ὃ φησι, inquit, λογικὴ ἀλόγος ψυχὴ γίνεται. Et quid aliud Aristoteles, dum incorruptibilem, immutabilem, immistum, simplicem, impartibilem, animum dixit, velle videtur, quàm ut immortalitatem rationi adscribat? 1. de anima: cap. 3. text. 49. cap. 4. text. 67. libr. 3. t. 6. 20. libr. 2. de gen. cap. 3. libr. 3. de part. anim. cap. 1. libr. 12. Metaph. ὑσν corrupto corpore ὑπομένειν dilucide satis ostendit. Videatur Scaliger, exerc. 307. sect. 20. Nicolaus Fabentinus de Immort. anim. cap. 11. Eugubinus libr. 9. de perenniphil. Porphyrius. D. Gregorius M. libr. 4. moral. cap. 7. Augustinus de quant. animæ. cap. 2. Lactant. libr. 7. cap. 8. 12. de irâ Dei. cap. 19. Macrob. in somn. Scip. libr. 2. cap. 13. & Oracula Sibyllina ubi inter alia effatum hoc divinissimum: Καὶ γάλα ἀμέμπτοις ... πάντασι δίκαιοις.
units.tr: This is the foundation and principle of salvation: that the nature of the soul is eternal and wholly exempt from the number of the Fates, says Palingenius, Zodiacus, Capricorn. Nor do we linger over those childish quibbles of Epicurus, Democritus, Dicaearchus, Pliny (Natural History, book 7, chapter 55), and the Machiavellians. Rather, it is permissible to approach and consult the wiser philosophers, even though they are pagans. With what force did Pythagoras, and his teacher Pherecydes, Trismegistus, Zoroaster, Numenius, and Plato in the Alcibiades, attack, indeed assail, that inhuman opinion of mad annihilation? Sallust, On the Gods and the World, chapter 20, says: [ὃ φησι] the irrational soul becomes rational. And what else does Aristotle seem to mean, when he calls the soul incorruptible, immutable, unmixed, simple, indivisible, than to ascribe immortality to reason? On the Soul, book 1, chapter 3, text 49; chapter 4, text 67; book 3, texts 6 and 20; On Generation, book 2, chapter 3; On the Parts of Animals, book 3, chapter 1; Metaphysics, book 12, clearly enough shows that it persists [ὑπομένειν] when the body is corrupted. Let Scaliger, Exercise 307, section 20; Nicolaus Fabrinus, On the Immortality of the Soul, chapter 11; Steuchus of Eugubium, book 9, On Perennial Philosophy; Porphyry; St Gregory the Great, Morals, book 4, chapter 7; Augustine, On the Greatness of the Soul, chapter 2; Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book 7, chapters 8 and 12; On the Anger of God, chapter 19; Macrobius, On the Dream of Scipio, book 2, chapter 13; and the Sibylline Oracles be consulted, where among other things this most divine saying occurs: [Καὶ γάλα ἀμέμπτοις ... πάντασι δίκαιοις]: "and milk to the blameless ... to all the just."

units.la: XXI. Duæ autem potissimum Facultates aut potentiæ, ex animæ rationalis naturâ emanant; quarum um prima est Intellectus, altera Voluntas. Suntque ambæ potentiæ corporis expertes, & ab omni materiâ sejunctæ. Hinc ab anima rationali, ut Physicus corpus informans actus est, non fluunt, nec earum operationes Physicæ sunt; quippe, quæ nec ratione subjecti, effecti, aut objectivæ nec formaliter sive terminative, cum naturali Ente communicent aut conveniant.
units.tr: XXI. Two faculties, or powers, arise chiefly from the nature of the rational soul: the first is the Understanding, the second the Will. Both powers are free from the body and separated from all matter. Hence they do not flow from the rational soul as the actuality that informs the body, as a physical form does, and their operations are not physical, since they share with a natural being neither in respect of subject, effect, or object, nor formally or terminatively.

units.la: XXII. Intellectus est potentia animæ intelligens, cognoscens & dijudicans actu ea, quæ sunt intelligibilia potentia. Arist. l. 3. de anima. c. 4. & 8.
units.tr: XXII. The Intellect is the power of the soul that understands, knows and actually judges those things which are intelligible in potency. Arist. l. 3. de anima. c. 4. & 8.

units.la: XXIII. Potentia est quoniam ab essentia cujus facultas est distinguitur, secus quam sit in Mente prima, in quâ solâ Intellectus idem est cum suâ essentiâ. Et hæc est nobilissima, ac vere divina illa proprietas, quæ homini reliquas substantias naturales omnes antestare largitur. Homini inquam tanquam subjecto totali, & composito; non animæ: hujus enim, quamdiu corpori informando affixa est effectum exiftit: At soluta à contagione materiæ jam tum subjectum intellectionis & voluntatis dicitur. Arist. lib. 1. de anima. t. 64.
units.tr: XXIII. A power is distinguished from the essence of which it is the faculty, except in the first Mind, in which alone the Intellect is the same as its essence. This is the most noble and truly divine property, which grants man to surpass all other natural substances. I say man, as the whole and composite subject, not the soul: for the soul, as long as it is attached to informing the body, exists as an effect; but once freed from the contagion of matter it is called the subject of understanding and willing. Arist. lib. 1. de anima. t. 64.

units.la: XXIV. Sunt verò illa potestate intelligibilia, vel corporalia, vel anima ipsa, eique inhærentia, vel substantiæ immateriales. Et corpora quidem cognitione immateriali, universali & necessariâ ab intellectu percipiuntur. Cognoscit is non essentialiter; tale enim scire soli Deo competit, cujus essentia immaterialiter omnium comprehensiva est: non per species naturaliter sibi inditas, aut à substantiis sive formis separatis effluxas; sed per phantasmata concepta & effecta. Unde per ligamentum sensuum non raro impediri in præsenti statu, qui nonnisi per comparationem ad sensibile, notum quid fieri, permittit, experimur. Ab iis igitur phantasmatibus abstrahit, per modum unius, materialia, & sensibilia, ac per ea in cognitionem immaterialium elevatur; ascendendo ab inferioribus ad superiora, ita ut primo sensus moveat Phantasiam, hæc poftmodum Intellectum, cui phantasma rei, imprimit rei speciem, de quâ receptâ judicium a ratione instituitur. Ex quo patet ab intellectu nô apprehendi per fe & principaliter singularia, quorum cognoscendorum via unica est Sensus, ut rectè Plato 6. de Republ. monuit. nec mentem actu aut habitu infinitorum, contingentium ac futurorum directè cognoscitivum esse. Contemplatur Intellectus dein semet-ipsum, & ea quæ in ipsius natura deprehendi advertit, non per effentiam, sed actum, qui est ipsum suum intelligere. Et tandem ea quæ sunt supera, illa vero in præfenti mortalitate non per seipsum, sed per rerum naturalium notitiam, uti docet Apostolus ad Rom. 1. & Avenpacem voluisse prodidit Avenroes, libr. 3. text. 36. Hinc ad perfectam Dei, mentiumque cognitionem unitæ corpori animæ pervenire impossibile esse deprehenditur. Plato in Cratylo. Fatendum est nos de Deo nihil cognoscere, neque de ipso atque ipsius nominibus, quibus seipsum vocat. Et Eurip. in Troadib. O Jupiter mortalibus non cognite Quis fis, utrumne Mentis, an Necessitas Natura.
units.tr: XXIV. Those things which are intelligible to this power are either bodies, or the soul itself and what inheres in it, or immaterial substances. Bodies are perceived by the intellect through immaterial, universal and necessary knowledge. It does not know them essentially, for such knowing belongs to God alone, whose essence immaterially comprehends all things. Nor does it know them through species naturally implanted in it, or emanating from separate substances or forms; but through phantasms conceived and formed. Hence we experience that in the present state it is not infrequently impeded by the binding of the senses, which allows us to know anything only by comparison with the sensible. The intellect therefore abstracts from those phantasms what is material and sensible, as it were by a single mode, and through them is raised to the knowledge of immaterial things, ascending from lower to higher. First the senses move the Phantasy, then the Phantasy moves the Intellect, on which the phantasm of the thing imprints the species of the thing, and from the species received reason forms a judgment. From this it is clear that singulars are not apprehended by the intellect through themselves and principally, since the only way of knowing them is sense, as Plato rightly warned in the sixth book of the Republic; nor is the mind, either actually or habitually, directly knowing of infinite, contingent and future things. The Intellect then contemplates itself, and those things it notices in its own nature, not through its essence but through its act, which is its very understanding. And finally, those things that are above, which in the present mortal state are known not through themselves but through knowledge of natural things, as the Apostle teaches in Rom. 1; and Averroes revealed that Avempace held this view, Averroes, lib. 3. text. 36. Hence it is found impossible for a soul united to a body to attain perfect knowledge of God and of minds. Plato in Cratylo: We must confess that we know nothing of God, neither of him nor of the names by which he calls himself. And Euripides in the Trojan Women: O Jupiter, unknown to mortals, whoever you are, whether the nature of mind or necessity.

units.la: Nec enim arte ulla, sed desuper solum revelari nobis incognofcibilem Deum, essentialiter fine lumine revelationis ac gratiæ constat. Idem cum Potino, Proclo, Magno Syriano. 2. libr. Metaph. ac Pythagoricis, asse-rit rit Orpheus, cui cognoscenti ejus incomprehensibilitatem in hymnis:
units.tr: Nor is it established that God, unknowable in his essence, is revealed to us by any art, but only from above, without the light of revelation and grace. Orpheus asserts the same, together with Plotinus, Proclus, Syrianus, the second book of the Metaphysics, and the Pythagoreans, acknowledging in his hymns God's incomprehensibility:

units.la: Nox principium universorum dictus est.
units.tr: "Night" is called the beginning of all things.

units.la: XXV. Causæ porrò intellectionis vel Instrumentales sunt, adeoque minus principales, Cor, Spiritus, & Imago; sive ea sit prima, proximè & immediatè: sive secunda, modum rem percipiendi repræsentans. Vel principales: quarum altera remotior, altera proximior est. Arist. lib. 3. de anima cap. 5. text. 18.
units.tr: XXV. The instrumental causes of intellection are, and so less principal, the heart, the spirit and the image, whether the image is the first, proximate and immediate, or the second, representing the manner of perceiving the thing. Or the principal causes, of which one is more remote and the other nearer. Arist. lib. 3. de anima cap. 5. text. 18.

units.la: XXVI. Remotior vis πνευματικὴ dicitur, estque vis quædam passiva remotè intellectionem causans, recipiendo & formando imaginem objecti intelligibilis.
units.tr: XXVI. The more remote power is called pneumatic [πνευματικὴ], and is a certain passive power that causes intellection remotely, by receiving and forming the image of the intelligible object.

units.la: XXVII. Passio autem illa non est remotio rei, secundum naturam ad esse, aut inclinationem convenientis, nec abjectio ejus, quod indiscriminatim, vel convenire, vel repugnare in naturâ positum habet: Sed est minus proprie patibilis affectio, quâ id quod potentiâ ad aliquid, illud ad quod erat in potentiâ sibi recipit, atque ita procedendo in actum intelligibilium, subjectum suum perficit.
units.tr: XXVII. That passion is not the removal of a thing, according to its nature, from its being or from its suitable inclination, nor the rejection of what it has in its nature to either agree or conflict with indiscriminately. It is rather a less properly passive affection, by which what is in potency to something receives into itself that to which it was in potency, and so, proceeding into the act of intelligibles, perfects its subject.

units.la: XXVIII. Receptio præterea imaginum, impressio sive formatio, vel Potentialis est, & hæc quidem cum purè & merè, tum καθ' ἕξιν talis, vel Actualis. Antonin. 1. part. sum. maj. l. 3. c. 1. ante §. 10.
units.tr: XXVIII. Moreover, the reception of images, their impression or formation, is either potential, and this is purely and simply so, or habitual [καθ' ἕξιν], or actual. Antonin. 1. part. sum. maj. l. 3. c. 1. ante §. 10.

units.la: XXIX. Prior possibilis sive patibilis mens, secundum naturam & essentiam suam considerata, infantum propria, nihil quicquam in se continet eorum, quæ intelligi possunt ac debent. Hinc Aristot. 3. de anima. cap. 4. Δεῖ, inquit, ὥσπερ ἐν γραμματείῳ, ὧν μηδὲν ὑπάρχει ἐντελεχείᾳ γεγραμμένον· ὅπερ συμβαίνει ἐπὶ τοῦ νοῦ. Et Plato scitè admodum l. 10. Phileb. in perf. Socr. libro eam in quem memoria cum sensibus incidens, verba quædam vera, verisve contraria inscribere, aut tanquam pictor imagines, pingere videatur, assimilat. Nec enim organorum inhabilitas jam tunc existens sensuum potentias ad extra exerceri permittit, à quibus alioquin mens formarum susceptiva ordinario physicoque modo movetur. Ipsa imago in intellectu ab Icone sensuali oboritur, in & ab anima illuminatur, cognoscitur, & à cognita aliæ notiones extrahuntur. Excipit namque intellectus noster species, vel extrinsecus perceptas, vel motu proprio ad similitudinem materialium effectas, immaterialiter penitus, fingit, & dijudicat: Adeoque causatur, ut, postquam à simulacro sensibili fusum est imaginabile, ab imaginabili feratur intelligibile; sicut à sole radii, à luce lumen spargitur.
units.tr: XXIX. The former, the possible or passive mind, considered according to its nature and essence, belongs to infants and contains nothing at all of those things which can and ought to be understood. Hence Aristotle, De anima 3, cap. 4: "It must be like a writing tablet on which nothing actually is written; which is what happens in the case of the mind." And Plato, very aptly in the Philebus, in Socrates' person, compares it to a book in which memory, meeting the senses, seems to inscribe certain true or contrary words, or, like a painter, to paint images. For the inability of the organs, already present at that time, does not allow the powers of the senses to be exercised outwardly, by which the receptive mind would otherwise be moved in the ordinary physical manner. The image itself arises in the intellect from the sensible icon, and in the soul it is illuminated and known, and other notions are drawn out from what is known. For our intellect receives species, either perceived from outside or produced by its own motion in likeness to material things, and forms and judges them wholly immaterially. And so it comes about that, after the imaginable has been poured out from the sensible simulacrum, the intelligible is carried over from the imaginable, just as light is spread from rays of the sun.

units.la: XXX. Altera habitualis differentia intellectus passivi, medio modo se habet, estque in actu primo; nec amplius ἀπλῶς potentia, cum nimirum nunc, ante apprehensa actu non intelliguntur. Et in hac quidem conservativa specierum intelligibilium vis, Memoria scil. intellectiva quàm maximè conspicitur. Si enim materia corporalis receptas formas non solùm tenet actu per eas agendo, sed etiam cessante actuali operationum emanatione: quid obstabit, quo minùs contra Avicennam intellectus dici possit, intelligibilium species receptas, five à sensibilibus five à superiori intellectu effluxas, conservare, etiam actu intellectione nulla existente. Hoc tamen discrimine observato, ut respectus temporis determinati, quæ determinatio particularium est, sensitivæ: indeterminatio intellectivæ memoriæ propria habeatur. XXXI. Postre-
units.tr: XXX. The other, habitual difference of the passive intellect holds a middle position: it is in first act, and no longer simply potency, since the things apprehended before are not understood in act at that moment. In this difference the conserving power of intelligible species, namely intellectual memory, is most clearly seen. For if corporeal matter not only holds received forms in act, by acting through them, but also retains them when the actual emanation of operations has ceased, what will prevent the intellect, against Avicenna, from being said to conserve received intelligible species, whether flowing from sensible things or from a higher intellect, even when no intellection is occurring? Yet this distinction must be observed: the respect for a determined time, which is the determination of particulars, belongs to the sensitive memory; indeterminacy is held to be proper to intellectual memory. XXXI. Postre-

units.la: XXXI. Postremò actualis sive Adeptus dicitur Intellectus is, qui est ἐνεργεία, adeoque in actu secundo, secundum completionem actûs ultimam. Et in hac quidem differentia, affectione illâ quam communem habet cum sensibus, ut Icones objectorum non nisi successivè producantur, retentâ; Entium quorumvis in potentiâ ad intellectionem existentium, imagines efformat: quæ efficiunt, ut intellectus impressione seu repræsentatione immateriali, cum speciebus intellectualibus unitus, singula, & intelligibilia esse dicatur, non aliter ac simulacrum in corpore denso perspicuo, ipsa res esse perhibetur secundum illud Scaligeri, Exerc.307.sect.37. Meditatio, frequens amatæ rei, eam etiam absentem unit cum intellectu: Non absque passione; quæ non tam ob habilitatem ac potentiam, quàm propter actuale pati, e receptione imaginis sensilis natum intellectui possibili accidit, nec propterea tendentiam ad ullam corruptibilitatem menti inducit, quin potius perfectiva est omnibus numeris absoluta.
units.tr: XXXI. Lastly, the intellect that is actual or adept is called that which is ἐνεργεία, and so in second act, according to its ultimate completion of act. In this difference, retaining the affection it shares with the senses, namely that the icons of objects are produced only successively, it forms images of whatever beings exist in potency to intellection. These bring it about that the intellect, united with intellectual species through an immaterial impression or representation, is said to be the singular and intelligible things themselves, just as a simulacrum in a dense, transparent body is said to be the thing itself, according to Scaliger: Exerc. 307, sect. 37. Meditation, frequent upon a beloved thing, unites it with the intellect even when it is absent. This is not without passion; which accrues to the possible intellect not so much from its capacity and power as from actual suffering, arising from the reception of a sensible image, and it does not therefore induce in the mind any tendency to corruptibility. Rather it is perfective and absolute in every respect.

units.la: XXXII. Notandum ultimò, Avicennam è recensione Lud. Cælii Rhodigini Lect. ant. libr. 2. cap. 1. intellectûs patientis statum quadruplicem constituere: adeò ut post eum, qui possibilitate tantum ceu potentia aliqua materialis, præditus est, dispositum ponat intellectum, qui principia per se nota jam continet, ipsi in habitu dictus; Cũ habitualis nobis fit, in quo res, actu speculationi nõ subjacet; Avicennæ Adeptus & perfectus adeoq; in tertiâ differentiarum serie collocatus. In hoc insuper discrepantes, quod hic adeptus actu speculans, ipsi accommodatus appellletur, adeoque quarta differentia constituatur. Liceat tamen priore retentâ distinctione Dispositum &
units.tr: XXXII. Finally, it should be noted that Avicenna, according to the edition of Lodovicus Caelius Rhodiginus, Lect. ant. libr. 2. cap. 1., sets up a fourfold state of the passive intellect. After the one who has only possibility, like a kind of material potency, he posits the disposed intellect, which already contains the principles known through themselves, and which is called habitual by him, in which the thing is not actually subject to speculation. Then comes the Adeptus of Avicenna, the perfect one, who is therefore placed in the third series of differences. They differ in this further point: that the adept who is actually speculating is called accommodated to it, and so a fourth difference is set up. Still, with the earlier distinction retained, it is allowed to say with the rest of the Scholastics that the disposed and the perfect are one and the same, even though the one contains conclusions and the other principles.

units.la: C Perfectum, etiamsi hic conclusiones, ille principia contineat cum reliquis Scholasticis unum eundemque dicere.
units.tr: Perfectum, although the one contains conclusions and the other principles, may be said with the rest of the Scholastics to be one and the same.

units.la: XXXIII. Altera mentis vis, quae intellectionis humanae principium propius est, activitatis ratio- nem magis obtinet.
units.tr: XXXIII. The other power of the mind, which is nearer to the principle of human understanding, has more of the character of activity.

units.la: Estque illa, quae species perceptas explicat, illustrat, dijudicat, & actu per abstractionem specierum a conditionibus materialibus intelligibiles reddit. Thom. l. 2. contra gent. cap. 77.
units.tr: It is the power that unfolds, illuminates and judges the species perceived, and by abstracting the species from their material conditions makes them actually intelligible. Thom. l. 2. contra gent. cap. 77.

units.la: XXXIV. Variè de ejus natura jam olim exitə- runt sententiæ.
units.tr: XXXIV. Opinions about its nature have varied from of old.

units.la: Veteres nonnulli facultatem eam esse putarunt, non a rationali, sed formâ longè diversâ emanantem. Plato 6. Repubi. Recentiores insuper vel omninò removerunt agentem animæ potetiam, ut Durandus 1. sentent. dist. 3. quæst. 5. vel intelligentiam primam, Zabarell. de mente agente. cap. 13. Alex. libr. 2. de anima. cap. 20. vel Genium, de quo Scal. libr. 3. Poet. cap. 16. Bodinus in Theat. nat. libr. 4. vel angelos universim; vel primam rerum inventionem, uti Melanchth. de anima, tract. 3. cap. 15. agens illud statuerunt. Verùm remotis absonis his, etsi præstantissimorum Philosophorum assertionibus, cum Aristot. libr. 3. de anima, cap. 5. ponamus: cùm præcipuè in intellectuali animæ nostræ naturâ, intrinsecum quodpiam lumen, quo potestate intelligibile, actu intelligibile reddi possit, necessariò requiratur; nec enim ulla actio, rei vitaliter competit, nisi per principium formaliter ei inhærens. Ac etsi Lumen divinum illustret mentem (attestante D. Johanne cap. 1. verf. 9. Jacobo cap. 1. v. 17. & Dionysio Areopag. qui Deum descripturus, libr. de divin. nomini. Ipsum bonum, inquit, lumine quovis excelsius, lumen intelligibile nuncupatur, tanquam fontana lux & exuberans profusio luminis intelleclu omnem super mundanum, circa mundanum, intra mundanum, sua illuminans plenitudine, totasq; intellectuales horum vires renovans, & omnes deniq; intellectus comprehendens, eo ipso quod se super eos expandit. Et Trismegisto in Asclepio. Una sola erat lux mentalis, ante lucem mentalem, & est semper mens mentis fulgida, & nihil aliud erat, quam hujus unitas, semper in seipsa existens, semper sua mete, luce & spiritu omnia continens.) humana, quæ ipsa quoque lux est: Unde in rationalibus creaturis præcipue imaginem Trinitatis conspicuam esse, cum in reliquis transiens tantummodo vestigium ejus deprehendatur, ex talibus quæ analogicè in divinas personas reduci queunt, docet D. Thomas 1. part. S. Theol. quæst. 79. artic. 4. Diversificantur tamen & essentiâ & operatione, cùm illud sit primum, summum, intransmutabile, invariabile, insensibile, non egenum, extra tempus, extra locum. Hoc verò earum proprietate nullâ, vel saltem improprie, dependenter ac instar simulacri insigne fit. Non nisi trans-naturales illud, tanquam hyperphysicum agens, quo immutatur in melius, lustratione non-naturali anima nostra sordibus peccati originalis coinquinata, operationes: hoc physicas in quovis intellectu etiam impientissimi hominis deprehensas perficit. Hæc genuina Aristotelis sententia est: etsi non negetur, eâ significatione, quâ ipsa anima à Deo esse dicitur, virtutem quoque intelligendi, à superiore illo perfectissimo, & præexistente immobili tanquam imperfectiorem, participatam ac mobilem, verùm mediatè dependere, eoque perfici ac beatificari. Nec minoris absurditatis illud delirium Avicenna qui 9. Metaph. cap. 4. Genium Cholcodæam mentem illustrare asseverat. itemque Melanchthonis opinio esse deprehenditur. Quamvis enim præstantissimam rerum inventionem, ipsosque Inventores summe sapientes esse, ipse Phil. in Transcendent. scient. lib. 1. cap. 1. affirmet, eo tamen reliquæ intellectus actiones tali causâ dignissimæ semovendæ nequaquam fuerunt.
units.tr: Some of the ancients thought that this faculty does not flow from the rational soul but from a quite different form. Plato, Republic 6. More recent writers have either removed altogether the agent power of the soul, as Durandus, Sentences 1, dist. 3, quaest. 5, or set up as the agent the first intelligence, as Zabarella, De mente agente, cap. 13; Alexander, De anima, libr. 2, cap. 20, or a genius, of whom Scaliger, Poetics libr. 3, cap. 16; Bodin, Theatre of Nature, libr. 4, or angels in general, or the first discovery of things, as Melanchthon, De anima, tract. 3, cap. 15. But setting aside these absurdities, and though we follow the assertions of the most distinguished philosophers, as Aristotle, De anima, libr. 3, cap. 5, since in the intellectual nature of our soul in particular some intrinsic light is necessarily required, by which what is intelligible in potency can be made intelligible in act; for no action properly belongs to a living thing except through a principle formally inhering in it. And although the divine light illumines the mind (as D. John, ch. 1, v. 9; James, ch. 1, v. 17; and Dionysius the Areopagite, who, about to describe God, says in On the Divine Names: "The Good itself, higher than any light, is called intelligible light, as a fountain-light and an overflowing outpouring of light, illuminating with its fullness the intellects above the world, around the world, and within the world, renewing their intellectual powers, and finally embracing all intellects by the very fact that it spreads itself over them." And Trismegistus in the Asclepius: "There was one mental light alone, before the mental light, and it is always the shining mind of the mind, and nothing else was but its unity, always existing in itself, always containing all things by its own mind, light and spirit."), still the human light, which is itself also light, is in rational creatures, in whom the image of the Trinity is especially visible, while in other creatures only a trace of it is found in passing, as D. Thomas, 1 part, S. Theol., quaest. 79, art. 4 teaches from things that can be analogically reduced to the divine persons. Yet they differ both in essence and in operation, since the one is first, highest, unchangeable, invariable, insensible, needing nothing, outside time and outside place. The other, by none of its properties, or at least only improperly, becomes remarkable as dependent and in the manner of an image. That light, as a hyperphysical agent, by which our soul, stained by the filth of original sin, is changed for the better, performs the operations not natural to it by a supernatural illumination; it perfects the physical operations found in any intellect, even that of the most impious man. This is the genuine opinion of Aristotle; although it is not denied that, in the sense in which the soul itself is said to be from God, the power of understanding also, participated in by the soul as something imperfect and mobile from that higher, most perfect and pre-existing immobile being, depends mediately upon it and is perfected and blessed by it. Nor is the delirium of Avicenna, who, Metaphysics 9, cap. 4, asserts that a genius illumines the mind of Cholcodaeus, of less absurdity; nor is the opinion of Melanchthon found to be different. For although he affirms, in Philippus, On the Transcendent Sciences, libr. 1, cap. 1, that the most excellent discovery of things and their inventors are supremely wise, the remaining actions of the intellect were by no means to be removed from such a worthy cause.

units.la: XXXV. Illuminat autem Objectum & intelligit illud, (sive fit externum, cujus Intellectio recta dicitur, quâ animus ad supera & infera se convertit; sive Internum, quæ reflexiva est, cũ intellectus in seipsum reflectitur) vel absolutè, vel comparatè Inveniendo aut Judicando.
units.tr: XXXV. Now the intellect illuminates its object and understands it, whether it is external, whose correct understanding is called intellection, by which the mind turns itself to things above and below, or internal, which is reflexive, when the intellect is reflected upon itself; and it does so either absolutely or comparatively, by finding or by judging.

units.la: XXXVI. Intellectus absolutus illuminat intelligibilia in mente capaci, de qua illustratione Sallustius de diis & mundo cap. 8. Τελεσμα ἐστιν δυναμις τῆς ψυχῆς ὥσπερ ἡλιος τὰς ὄψεις. Architas apud Jamblichium lib. 2. de secta Pythag. c. 4. Proclus in Tim. lib. 4. Trismeg. 5. serm. Pim. Hom. 3. Iliad. &c. scrutatur simulacra illa, enucleat, investigat, & fine ullo tandem examine apprehendit. Idque facit vel in simplici, cujus Intellectio cum Abstractiva, tum Constitutiva appellari convenienter potest; vel in dependenti, & conjuncta mentis Icone.
units.tr: XXXVI. The absolute intellect illumines intelligibles in a capable mind, concerning which illumination Sallust, On the Gods and the World, cap. 8 says: "The end is a power of the soul, as the sun is of the eyes" [Τελεσμα ἐστιν δυναμις τῆς ψυχῆς ὥσπερ ἡλιος τὰς ὄψεις]. Archytas, as cited by Iamblichus, On the Pythagorean Life, libr. 2, cap. 4; Proclus, On the Timaeus, libr. 4; Trismegistus, 5th sermon; Pimander, Homily 3; Iliad, etc. It searches those images, brings them out, investigates them, and finally grasps them without any further examination. It does this either in the simple case, whose intellection can fittingly be called both abstractive and constitutive, or in the dependent case, which is joined to the icon of the mind.

units.la: XXXVII. Posterior Proba est, sive Examen Intellectionis prioris, quâ intelligitur, qua ratione in cognitionem imaginis pervenerit intellectus, quomodo abstraxerit, adhibuerit ve Causas, propria, partes, quæ intra: vel Objecta, Adjuncta, &c. quæ extrinsecus eminent, & tandem quâ ratione Ens cum alio à seipso dispositum sit. Atque ita suas actiones omnes ad principiorum canonumq; normam, quibus omnibus Logica artificialis præcipuè, post obscuratum intellectus nostri lumen, adjumento esse potest, fideliter exigit; idque vel simpliciter vel comparaté.
units.tr: XXXVII. The latter is a proof, or examination of the prior intellection, by which it is understood by what method the intellect has come to the knowledge of the image, how it abstracted, and what causes it employed, whether proper, parts that lie within, or objects and adjuncts that stand out externally; and finally by what method a being is disposed together with another distinct from itself. And so it faithfully brings all its actions to the rule of principles and canons, by which all of artificial logic, especially after the light of our intellect was obscured, can be of help; and this either simply or comparatively.

units.la: XXXVIII. Quare duæ hæ Intellectus actívi virtutes, Inventio, & Judicium distinctæ rationis functiones sunt. Nec respectu tantum, aut ratione aliquâ inter se differunt, uti perperam sentit Keckerm. Syst. Phys. libr. 4. cap. 4. de intell. act. §. 6. Ita enim is: Inventio & Judicium non sunt partes sed causa intellectionis humanæ, atque adeo sunt reipsâ unum & idem, dupliciter tantum considerata. Probationem vel nullam vel topicam saltem addere satagit. Quamvis enim detur, circa eandem intellectionem utramque facultatem versari, ex eo tamen diversitas partialis nondum sublata est, utpote cum ultró etiam ipsi hoc largiri possimus, eandem esse utrique materiam circa quam, Genericam videlicet: In uno enim omnes partes consentire convenit. Negatur verò objecti, specifici identitas, de qua est quæstio.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Therefore these two powers of the active intellect, invention and judgment, are distinct functions of reason. Nor do they differ from each other merely in respect or in some way, as Keckermann, Systema Physicae, libr. 4, cap. 4, de intellectu activo, §6, wrongly thinks. For he says: "Invention and judgment are not parts but causes of human intellection, and so they are really one and the same, considered only in two ways." He tries to add a proof, either none or at least a topical one. For although it be granted that both faculties are concerned with the same intellection, the partial diversity has not yet been removed by this, since we can willingly concede to him that the matter about which they are both concerned is the same, namely the generic matter; for it is agreed that all parts agree in one. But the identity of the specific object, which is the question, is denied.

units.la: XXXIX. Hæc de primâ Intellectus divisione, se- quitur altera, è ratione modi intelligendi orta, se- cundum quem Intellectio simplex est, vel Com- posita. XL. Simplex intellectio est, cujus cognitione in- complexæ rerum notiones continentur. Estque pri- maria hæc longeque perfectior composita, cùm ho- mo Dei imaginem eâ repræsentet, ipsosque ange- los, (in quibus perfecta est, secundùm insitæ sibi na- turæ modum, quem transcendere non datur, cogni- tio intelligibilis veritatis. Dionys. 7. cap. de divin. nom. cap. 7.) quam convenientissimè, utpote quâ ipsa rei essentiâ, & quid res fit cognoscitur, imitari videatur. XLI. Composita est, quæ incomplexos conce- ptus componit, Idque facit, vel simpliciori notio- num connexione, quæ Propositio, & συνθετος intelle- ctus dicitur: Cùm sine discurrente vi duæ intentio-
units.tr: XXXIX. So much for the first division of the intellect. There follows another, arising from the manner of understanding, by which intellection is either simple or composite. XL. Simple intellection is that in which the notions of things are contained as incomplex concepts. This is the primary and far more perfect kind, since man by it represents the image of God, and it seems to imitate most fittingly the angels themselves (in whom, according to the mode of their innate nature, which cannot be transcended, intelligible knowledge of truth is perfect. Dionys. 7. cap. de divin. nom. cap. 7.), since by it the very essence of a thing and what the thing is are known. XLI. Composite is that which combines incomplex concepts. It does this either by the simpler connection of notions, which is called a proposition and "synthetic intellect" [συνθετος intellectus], when two intentions

units.la: nes conjunctione, aut divisione unicâ disponuntur: Vel magis compositâ, quæ Ratio proprie dicitur, cùm intellectus ab intellecto uno, ad aliud transiens, denarium noematum numerum exsuperat: Quod operatione dianoetica sive discursu, & agitatione mentis, vel illative, vel ordinative fieri amat.
units.tr: are arranged by a single conjunction or division, without discursive force; or by the more complex connection, which is properly called reasoning, when the intellect, passing from one act of understanding to another, exceeds the number of ten notions. This it likes to do by dianoetic operation or discourse, and by the stirring of the mind, either illatively or orderly.

units.la: XLII. Illativus mentis discursus, Ratiocinatio & λογισμὸς dictus, ex trium noematum compositione consequentiam deducit formaliter necessariam, adeoque vel opinionem, vel scientiam causatur. XLIII. Ordinativus orationem pluribus constantem pronunciatis, axiomaticè dispositam, & si quâ opus ad syllogisticî discursus limam examinatam, naturæ industriâ artificiosè logico opitulante, in ordinem redigit. XLIV. Tertia Intellectûs distinctio est ratione Objectorum, seu potius finis, in Contemplativum & Practicum. Arist. 6. Ethic. cap. 1. lib. 3. de anima. c. 8. Scal. exerc. 307. sect. 23. qui à se invicem ipsâ naturâ non sejuncti sunt: accidentali respectu ad objectum, Entia per se non diversificante. Accidit namque solummodo apprehenso, ut ad opus ulterius suscipiendū vel intendatur, vel ab actione insequeti remittatur. XLV. Speculativus sive Theoreticus est, qui operatur solius cognitionis, intentione, quâ terminatur, apprehenso nô ordinato ad opus, sed veritatis duntaxat intellectionem. XLVI. Objectum ejus est Ens necessariû, & quod ab actione propterea nostrâ non dependet. Estque notitiæ theoreticæ productivus, utpote qui notitiarum illarum, five principiorum nobis aliquomodo innatorum, (ad quæ etiam fine ratiocinatione rapimur, & à quibus simpliciter intellectis, secundum viam acquisitionis vel inventionis ratiocinatio tanquam ab immobili termino, ad quietum procedit, & in via judicii ad prima illa principia, resolvendo revertitur, Jope ac fundamine contemplatur Veritate, & Verum quod intellectûs, cujus præcipuus civis est, terminus existit. Arist. 2. Metaph. c. 1. 2. post. Anal. cap. 19. Thom. 1. part. S. Th. quæst. 16. art. 1.
units.tr: XLII. Illative discourse of the mind, called reasoning and "logismos" [λογισμὸς], draws a formally necessary consequence from the composition of three notions, and so causes either opinion or science. XLIII. The ordinative discourse arranges in order an oration made up of several propositions, axiomatically disposed, and, if anything is needed, examined by the file of syllogistic discourse, with the help of natural industry skilfully aided by logic. XLIV. The third distinction of the intellect is by reason of its objects, or rather its end, into contemplative and practical. Arist. 6. Ethic. cap. 1. lib. 3. de anima. c. 8. Scal. exerc. 307. sect. 23. These are not separated from one another by nature itself; the difference is accidental with respect to the object, which does not diversify beings per se. For it happens only to what is apprehended, whether it is to be taken up for further work or is relaxed from the action that follows. XLV. The speculative or theoretical intellect is that which operates only for the sake of knowledge, its intention being that by which it terminates: the apprehended is not ordered to work, but only to the intellection of truth. XLVI. Its object is necessary being, which therefore does not depend on our action. It is productive of theoretical knowledge, since it resolves back, as to first principles, to those notions or principles that are in some way innate to us (to which we are carried even without reasoning, and from which, once simply understood, reasoning proceeds by the way of acquisition or discovery, as from an immovable term, to what is at rest, and by the way of judgment resolves back to those first principles). With their aid and foundation it contemplates truth, and the true, which is the proper term of the intellect, is its chief citizen. Arist. 2. Metaph. c. 1. 2. post. Anal. cap. 19. Thom. 1. part. S. Th. quæst. 16. art. 1.

units.la: XLVIII. Practicus est, cujus intellectio & ratiocinatio propter opus, ac Bonum efficiendum fuscipitur.
units.tr: XLVII. The practical intellect is that whose intellection and reasoning is undertaken for the sake of the work and the good to be brought about.

units.la: XLVIII. Circa Objectum versatur tale; quod aliter se habere potest, & à voluntate humana dependet. Notitiam practicam, quæ post cognitionem ulteriorem, ad quam ordinata est, operationem exigit, producit.
units.tr: XLVIII. It is concerned with an object that can be otherwise and depends on the human will. It produces practical knowledge, which, after the further knowledge to which it is ordered, demands an operation.

units.la: XLIX. Conducit autem operatio illa practica vel ad mores hominum, unde Moralis dicitur, innixa principio Legis naturæ, & recto rationis dictamini, unde Assensus ortum accipit: vel è mente factiva emanat, quæ dependentia nomen eiactionis Artificialis indit.
units.tr: XLIX. That practical operation leads either to the conduct of men, whence it is called moral, resting on the principle of the law of nature and the right dictate of reason, from which assent takes its origin; or it issues from the productive mind, and this dependence gives it the name of artificial action.

units.la: L. Et hæc tandem omnia intellectui insunt, vel liberè se habenti, remque aut certò scienti, aut dubitandi opinantive, ac ob infirmitatem accidentem labascenti: Vel strictè, dum intellectioni, alienæ propriæve, præteritæ tamen intentus, cogitata resolvit ac recognoscit.
units.tr: L. All these things are present in the intellect either when it is freely disposed and knows the matter with certainty, or when it doubts and holds opinions, and wavers through accidental weakness; or strictly, when, intent on another's understanding or its own past understanding, it resolves and recognises its thoughts.

units.la: Hac de Intellectu humano.
units.tr: Thus concerning the human intellect.

units.la: DEO TRINO, ET UNI, LAUS, HONOR ET GLORIA.
units.tr: TO THE TRIUNE AND ONE GOD, PRAISE, HONOUR AND GLORY.

units.la: Ad Ornatissimum Dn. Respondentem.
units.tr: To the Most Distinguished Sir, the Respondent.

units.la: FABRITI nostræ quondam pars maxima mentis, Nec nunc diviso corpore, crede, minor! Ut veniens à Te me nuper epistola grata, Et multum votis ante petita meis. Illa ut me docuit specimen Te grande laboris, Auctusq; in studiis edere velle Tui. Extemplo, solitæ gnarus virtutis & artis, Exilii, in tales os solüiq; sonos.
units.tr: Once, you were the greatest part of my mind, and, believe me, you are no less now that our bodies are apart. Your pleasant letter reached me lately, one I had long sought in my prayers. It taught me that you give a great sample of your labour and wish to grow in your studies. At once, knowing your accustomed virtue and skill, I loosed my mouth into such sounds, though I was in exile.

units.la: FABRITIUS nostrum dum sedulus intellectum Instituit celsâ disserere è cathedrâ, Non tam quantum nos, sed quantū intellegat ipse, Notum facundo cuilibet ore facit.
units.tr: While our Fabritius diligently sets out the intellect from a lofty chair, he makes known to anyone, with an eloquent mouth, not so much how much we understand as how much he himself understands.

units.la: Amico probato, & constanti,
units.tr: To a approved and constant friend,

units.tr: Congratulates him on the success of his studies, and at the same time bears witness to the faith of their old friendship.
